artifact.self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer k ≥ 1 and a finite alphabet Σ. Two finite words u, v ∈ Σ* are said to be k-abelian equivalent, written u ∼_k v, if |u| = |v| and, for every word w ∈ Σ* with |w| ≤ k, the number of occurrences of w as a factor of u equals the number of occurrences of w as a factor of v. For an integer n ≥ 2, a finite word W is called a strongly k-abelian n-th power if W can be written as a concatenation W = w_1 w_2 ⋯ w_n of n nonempty words of equal length such that w_i ∼_k w_1 for every i = 1, …, n.

Determine, as a function of the length N (and of |Σ|, k, n), the number f(N) of words in Σ^N that contain at least one factor which is a strongly k-abelian n-th power. More precisely, give an exact formula or a sharp asymptotic estimate for f(N), and analogously for the number of words in Σ^N that are themselves strongly k-abelian n-th powers.
artifact.status_search_result: Strongly k-abelian powers are an active research topic in combinatorics on words. Surveys on abelian combinatorics on words (e.g., the 2022 survey by Ridon/Whiteland and related work) discuss avoidability of strongly k-abelian n-th powers but do not report exact counting formulas for the number of length-N words containing such a power. No source found that resolves the enumeration problem, so it appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Abelian combinatorics on words: A survey
status_evidence.snippet: Survey discusses k-abelian equivalence, strongly k-abelian powers, and related avoidability/complexity questions; does not give an exact count of length-N words containing a strongly k-abelian n-th power.
status_evidence.claim: Counting question for strongly k-abelian powers is not resolved in the surveyed literature.

status_evidence.title: Strongly k-Abelian Repetitions
status_evidence.snippet: Introduces strongly k-abelian n-th powers and studies avoidability rather than enumeration.
status_evidence.claim: Foundational paper defines strongly k-abelian powers but leaves enumeration open.
